role: Naan baker at an old-town naan shop
headline: Five years an apprentice since he walked in at nineteen, the naan baker at a shop that has stood for over twenty years in Urumqi's old town, who lights the tandoor oven at half past four every morning and slaps the dough onto its walls with one arm reaching into a 300-degree mouth
unit: A naan shop in the old town of Tianshan district, Urumqi, open for more than twenty years (shop at the front, bakehouse at the back, two tandoor ovens)
level: You can mix the dough, pinch off the portions, stamp the patterns and bake on your own, and a batch of onion naan comes out even. You still need the old master to call out a word about the heat, and you haven't yet run the oven for the big naan or the butter naan
intro: The old master's back has been bad this year, and the fire in the first oven has been handed to you. At half past four in the morning you push up the shutter; the streetlights in the old town are still on. You toss a handful of water into the oven and listen to it hiss. As of today, the first batch of naan this shop sells each morning is yours.
salary_note: Estimate: at an old-town naan shop in Urumqi, a baker gets a monthly wage plus commission and one meal a day, a little below the national figure for bakers. At shops that have started selling online or moved into an industrial park, the skilled jobs can pay upper-middle.

day: Push up the shutter, open the gas valve, light the oven. While the walls heat through, you lift last night's dough out of the proofing cabinet and press it; the dent slowly rises back. Ready.
Mix the second tub. Fifty kilos of flour into the mixer, salt water, yeast and oil in the old master's proportions; onions chopped fine and squeezed dry, set aside to knead into the dough.

The first batch. Pinch, roll into a ball, press into a round, thin in the middle and thick at the rim, stamp a ring of pattern with the naan stamp, brush on weak salt water, scatter sesame. Over a padded cushion you slap them one by one onto the oven wall, and the sleeve guard on your arm is already stiff with heat.

With an iron hook you lift the naan out one by one and stack them on the wooden rack by the door. Schoolkids take one each, the owner of the noodle place next door carries off twenty at a time, and a taxi driver pulls up at the curb and calls out for two hot ones.

The online orders have printed: three to Guangzhou, two to Hangzhou, one to Chengdu. Naan has to be completely cool before it's packed, so you run stack after stack through the vacuum sealer, stick on the shipping labels and wait for the courier at noon.
The hottest hour in the shop. You lie for half an hour on the bench in the back room, watching videos other naan shops have posted on your phone, checking how well they stamp their patterns.
The second wave in the afternoon: people off work, tourists browsing the bazaar. A woman orders big naan for a toy, a wedding, on Sunday: twenty of them, a full half meter across.
Shut the oven, rake out the ash, wipe the cushions. Tomorrow's dough set to rise, the onions peeled. You take one last look at the embers at the oven mouth and pull down the shutter.

ladder.title: Naan Apprentice
ladder.focus: Tend the fire, mix dough, pinch off portions, haul flour, wash the cushions, and watch the master bake. You get to the oven on strong hands, early mornings, and dough balls that all come out the same size.

ladder.title: Naan Baker (Chinese Pastry Cook, Level 4)
ladder.focus: Mix, stamp, bake and pull out the naan on your own, dozens to a batch, all evenly colored. You move up on consistent batches, speed, and handling all the everyday kinds of naan.

ladder.title: Oven Master (Chinese Pastry Cook, Level 3)
ladder.focus: Run one oven and two or three people: set the dough formula, read the heat, plan the order of batches; the big naan, the butter naan and the banquet orders are all yours. You move up on steady color, a good name, and turning out apprentices.

ladder.title: Naan Bakery Technical Supervisor (Chinese Pastry Technician)
ladder.focus: With the shop grown into several branches, own every branch's dough formulas, new products and baker training, and write what's in your hands down as standards. You move up on new products that sell and branches that don't drift from the taste.

ladder.title: Naan Bakery Technical Director (Senior Technician)
ladder.focus: Run the central bakehouse and the frozen naan dough line, food safety and recipes, and decide products with the owner. You hold the job on the taste of the name over the door and how much ships.

ai_tasks.name: Checking ingredient quality and preparing the oven
ai_tasks.how: AI and sensors can help log ingredient stock, flag use-by dates, and monitor oven temperature and preheating. But whether the flour smells off, whether the oil has turned, where the oven heats unevenly, still has to be judged and decided by a person's eyes, nose and hands.

ai_tasks.name: Kneading, cutting and shaping the dough
ai_tasks.how: Kneading, dividing and shaping come down to feel, adjusting all the time to how firm, warm and risen the dough is. At most AI offers recipe and process references; the hands-on work still has to be done by a person.

ai_tasks.name: Putting the bread into the oven to bake
ai_tasks.how: Smart ovens can control temperature and time by program and sound an alert when it's done, and AI vision can help judge the color. But when to load, the steam, the arrangement and the call on doneness when it comes out are still made by a person reading the actual bread.

events.e_arm_burn: Rushing the morning batch, your wrist touched the oven mouth and rose in a string of blisters. The old master took one look and brought out a tin of burn cream he'd used for over ten years, and said: quick hands, not a hurried heart.
events.e_first_big: For the first time you baked a big naan on your own: a round of dough half a meter across, held up in both hands and slapped onto the oven wall. It didn't fall, didn't slip. When it came out, the master held it to the light to look at the pattern, then put it in the most prominent spot by the door.
events.e_gas_kang: Every naan oven in the old town has been converted to gas or electric; no more coal or charcoal. The first week, the bottoms of your naan kept coming out pale. The master said the fire is the same fire, it just has a different temper, and you'd have to get to know it again.
events.e_video: A tourist filmed you baking and posted it online, with the moment your arm reaches into the oven in slow motion. For that whole month there were phones held up at the door every day, and online orders tripled.
events.e_flour: A new batch of flour had different gluten, and a whole tub of dough over-proved and sagged on the oven wall. You threw out half the tub and reworked the water and salt for the new flour, and that day's naan came out an hour late.
events.e_love: The young woman from the dried fruit shop across the road bought a sesame naan every morning, then two, and then said your patterns were prettier than other shops'. You started stamping an extra ring on hers.
events.e_winter: Mornings at twenty below, and the queue at the door breathing white clouds. By the oven you're hot enough to work in a vest, and when you turn to hand naan out the door, the cold wind pours down your collar. That winter you coughed for over a month.
events.e_wedding_self: You got married. You baked the big naan for your own toy, thirty of them, each with a different pattern. The master sat at the top table, ate a mouthful and nodded.
events.e_smart_kang: The shop installed an electric naan oven with temperature control: a screen shows the wall temperature and it beeps on time. The new apprentice bakes to the screen and the naan don't burn anymore, but where to place each one on the wall, you still taught him one by one.
events.e_back: Bending over hundreds of times a day, your back finally gave out, and one morning you couldn't straighten up. You lay at home for a week, and your junior took over your oven.
events.e_child: Your child was born. On the day the baby turned one month old you baked a batch of tiny butter naan and took them door to door to the neighbors, each stamped with a little circle.
events.e_express: One summer a box of naan to Guangzhou spent five days on the road, and the customer said it had gone moldy and left a bad review. You refunded them, and from then on in summer you only shipped where it would arrive in two days, with an extra oxygen absorber in the pack.
events.e_contest: The city held a naan-baking skills competition, and you baked a dimpled naan with rose jam, its pattern stamped in the shape of a pomegranate. You took first prize, and the certificate hangs behind the counter where you take the money.
events.e_master_retire: The master stopped working and went home to look after his grandchildren. The day he left, he put the naan stamp he'd used for thirty years on your board, its wooden handle worn to a shine, and said nothing.
events.e_stock_ai: The owner installed stock-and-sales software: it warns when flour, sesame or onions are running low, and works out from last month's sales how many tubs of dough to mix tomorrow. It's pretty accurate, it just doesn't know there's a wedding on Sunday.
events.e_house: You put down a deposit on a flat in Midong district, and every morning at four you ride your e-bike into town. In winter there's no one on the roads but the snowplows, and you wear two masks.
events.e_apprentice: The new apprentice's dough balls were all different sizes. You didn't shout. You gave him a scale and had him weigh every one he pinched. After a month of weighing, he didn't need the scale.
events.e_tourist_slow: One year the tourists were strangely few, and half the shops on the bazaar street were shuttered. Online orders fell too. The owner paid three months of base wages only, and you shut down one oven.
events.e_parents: Your father went into hospital. By day you sat at his bedside; at three in the morning you went back to the shop, baked the first batch, then rode back to the hospital. The nurses thought you worked nights.
events.e_old_customer: An old neighbor who moved east more than ten years ago came back to visit family, took a taxi from the airport straight to the shop door, bought an onion naan and ate it standing up. That's the taste, he said, and took ten more with him.
events.e_line: The big factory in the industrial park has a fully automatic naan line: pressing, stamping, baking, all by machine, thousands an hour. You went on a visit once. The machine-stamped patterns were very neat, every one exactly the same.
events.e_shoulder: After more than twenty years of reaching into the oven, your shoulder hurts when you raise it high. You've handed the top ring of the oven wall to your apprentice and bake the lower two rings yourself.

c_cert.title: Sit the Level 3 Chinese pastry certificate or not
c_cert.situation: The district vocational training center has started an advanced course in Chinese pastry. A Level 3 certificate brings a yearly skills subsidy, and the shop will look at it when it picks an oven master later. The course is a month of classes, all in the afternoon, exactly when you catch up on sleep.

options.label: Sign up and sit it
options.result: You went to classes in the afternoons and memorized food safety questions at night. The practical was flower rolls and leavened flatbread, and yours came out looking like naan. The teacher laughed, and passed you anyway.

options.label: Skip it, sleep a little longer
options.result: You still lie on the bench in the back room in the afternoons. No certificate, but the regulars all know whose hands baked the first batch each morning.

c_online.title: Build up the online shop or not
c_online.situation: The owner's nephew wants to grow the shop's online store: videos, livestreams, vacuum-packed naan shipped to the rest of China. He wants you baking in front of the camera every afternoon, with an extra batch just for shipping.

options.label: Go along with it
options.result: You baked in front of the camera. At first your hands shook; later you forgot the camera was there. After a year the online orders outnumbered what sold at the door, and your commission went up with them.

options.label: Stick to the counter at the door
options.result: You said the naan in your hands is for the people at the door. The nephew found another baker for the videos, and you went on doing two batches a day and getting a full sleep in the afternoons.

c_kang.title: The Oven Master's place
c_kang.situation: The old master says one more year and he's going home, and the first oven needs someone to run it: the dough formula, the heat and the banquet orders all go to the oven master. The other baker in the shop came three years before you, and his big naan are better than yours.

options.label: Go for it
options.result: Every day you mixed one extra tub and tried the master's proportions one by one, noting them in a little book of your own. Before he left, the old master handed you the first oven, and the other baker later went to another shop.

options.label: Let him go first
options.result: He took the first oven and you kept the second. His big naan are good, your butter naan are good, the two ovens work one behind the other, and the queue at the door got longer.

c_factory.title: Go to the big factory in the industrial park
c_factory.situation: A big factory in the industrial park that makes frozen naan dough is poaching people. It wants a baker who knows handmade naan to tune the dough formula on its production line. Twenty percent more pay, eight hours, weekends off; only you'd face machines all day and never bake another naan.

options.label: Go to the factory
options.result: You put on a white coat and adjusted the dough formula in the lab over and over, until the machine-pressed rounds rose with that ring of rim too. At weekends you go back to the old shop and borrow your junior's oven for a batch; your hands haven't lost it.

options.label: Stay at the shop
options.result: You turned it down. That afternoon you stood by the oven a little longer, watching the last naan slowly puff up.

c_inland.title: A Xinjiang restaurant in Shanghai
c_inland.situation: A Xinjiang restaurant in Shanghai is opening a branch and wants you as its naan baker, offering half again what you earn now, with lodging. You'd be on your own over there, baking every day for people who don't know what naan is.

options.label: Go to Shanghai
options.result: You bake in a glass room in the restaurant, and diners film you through the glass. The flour is different in Shanghai, the water too, and it took a month to get the taste right. Every New Year you fly back to Urumqi, and the first thing you do off the plane is eat a naan at the old shop.

options.label: Stay in Urumqi
options.result: You didn't go. That winter you added a pumpkin naan at the shop, and the old neighbors said it was good and asked you to make it again next year.

c_own_shop.title: Open a naan shop of your own
c_own_shop.situation: You've saved a little. Your wife says your skills are ready, and there's a shopfront at the gate of a new housing compound out in Midong; why not open your own? The owner hears about it and offers a higher commission, saying the shop can't do without you.

options.label: Open your own
options.result: You built an oven and hung up a sign, and at four in the morning you open the door yourself, light the fire yourself, take the money yourself. You lost a little in the first six months; later everyone in the compound knew your naan.
options.end: You opened your own naan shop at the gate of a housing compound in Midong: one oven, shop at the front, bakehouse at the back. Every morning, from the first batch, the compound's children each take one on the way to school.

options.label: Stay for the higher commission
options.result: You stayed. The owner hung a photo of you baking behind the counter, captioned: Our baker.

c_tech.title: Apply for Naan Bakery Technical Supervisor
c_tech.situation: The shop has grown to four branches, and the owner wants one person to own every branch's dough formulas, new products and baker training: the Naan Bakery Technical Supervisor. Will you apply? It means writing recipes, filling in spreadsheets and running between shops, and half the time by the oven gone.

options.label: Apply
options.result: You copied the formulas from your little book into spreadsheets, writing for each naan the grams, the proving time and the oven temperature, and added a last line: look at the dough, listen to the oven. The owner read it and said from next month all four shops follow this.

options.label: Don't apply, keep the oven
options.result: The owner found a young man to handle the recipes, and you still light the oven before dawn every day. When the young man can't get a dough right, he comes and stands by you for a while.

c_teach.title: Teach naan baking at the training center
c_teach.situation: The district vocational training center runs a naan-baking course and asks you to teach young people who want to learn a trade. A fixed salary, winter and summer holidays, no getting up before dawn, a bit less money than now.

options.label: Go and teach
options.result: You stand at the electric oven in the training kitchen showing twenty young people how to pinch off dough, weighing every one, the way you once taught your apprentices.
options.end: You became the naan-baking teacher at the training center, turning out dozens of trainees a year; some went home to their villages and opened naan shops, and at New Year they send you a photo of the sign over the door.

options.label: Stay by the oven
options.result: You said a few more years. The center left a letter of appointment, and you slid it under the glass on the counter where you take the money.

c_director.title: A central bakehouse: become Naan Bakery Technical Director or not
c_director.situation: The owner is building a central bakehouse in the industrial park to make frozen naan dough for the branches and for supermarkets, and wants you as Naan Bakery Technical Director, running the line, food safety and the recipes. You'd be at the bakehouse every day, and the old shop's oven would go to your apprentice.

options.label: Take it
options.result: Every day you tune formulas at the line, read the test reports and sit in meetings with the owner. Of every batch of machine-pressed dough, you insist on taking one back to the old shop's oven, and if it doesn't bake right, it doesn't ship.

options.label: Put your apprentice forward
options.result: You pushed your apprentice up and kept the old shop's first oven yourself. Back from meetings, he often brings a round of dough over for you to look at.

endings.retire: On the last day you still pushed up the shutter at half past four in the morning, tossed a handful of water into the oven and listened to it hiss. The first batch you baked was onion naan, the same as the day you took over the oven more than thirty years ago. After shutting down you wiped clean the naan stamp the master left you and set it on your apprentice's board, without a word.
endings.burnout: That winter your shoulder wouldn't lift at all, and your arm couldn't reach into the oven mouth. You only heard half of what the doctor said. You told the owner you were done and handed the oven to your apprentice. Later, when a neighbor's family held a wedding, they'd still ask you over to check the patterns on the big naan were right.

stages: Of the two ovens, the second is yours. Early each morning you mix, pinch and press, stamp the patterns, slap the rounds one by one onto the oven wall over a padded cushion, and hook them out one by one with the long iron hook; onion naan, sesame naan, dimpled naan, you can turn out on your own. When the old master calls out a word from the first oven about the heat, you turn the gas valve down a touch.

The first oven is yours now, and the dough formula with it. You decide how many tubs to mix today, how much salt in the water, which batch is the big naan, and you take the banquet orders too: how many for the wedding, how big, what pattern. With two apprentices, one pinching dough and one watching the oven, you stand between them, baking while you watch their hands; if a batch comes out uneven, it's on you.

Four shops' dough formulas are yours to manage. You visit three a week and stand by each oven a while, looking at the dough balls, tasting the naan; new products you work out tub by tub in the old shop's back room, rose jam, pumpkin, walnut, then write up as recipe sheets for the branches. New bakers learn from you for a month, and only go on an oven once you've signed off.

Most of your time is at the central bakehouse in the industrial park: the line, the deep freeze, the test lab. You meet the owner and supermarket buyers, read the test report for every batch of dough, set the recipes and shelf lives; when food safety inspectors come, you walk them through the plant. Once a week you still go back to the old shop, take one round off the line and bake it in the first oven.
work: The owner of a noodle place orders a hundred small naan, one ring smaller than usual. You take the dough balls from 200 grams down to 150, and when the first batch comes out he holds one against the edge of a noodle bowl and says: just right.

The oven wall is coloring unevenly today, always scorching on the left. You shine a torch into the oven for ages and find a ring of burner holes clogged, clear them bit by bit with a wire, and the next batch comes out even.

An online customer says the old folks at home have weak teeth and wants a softer naan. You add milk and an egg to the dough, bake it two minutes less, and break off a piece to taste yourself before it ships.

Sunday's wedding needs thirty big naan, so you set the dough the day before and light the oven at three in the morning. Thirty big naan slapped on one by one and hooked off one by one; when the last one comes out, it's just getting light.
The new apprentice's naan keep sliding down the wall. You stand behind him, press his wrist and slap one onto the wall with him, saying: not pushing up, pressing in. The next one stays.

The flour mill changed its packaging. You still grab a fistful and rub it between your fingers, sniff it, and mix a small bowl to test. It rises slower than the last batch, so you add an extra spoon of yeast to this tub.

The regulars at the north-side shop say the naan isn't right. You stand there one morning and see the baker is rushing, cutting the proof twenty minutes short. You don't say anything to him in the shop; back home, you put the proofing time on the recipe sheet in bold.

Testing a walnut naan, you go through seven tubs of dough in the old shop's back room: too much walnut and the naan cracks, too little and you can't taste it. When the seventh batch comes out, you break off a piece for the owner. He eats it without a word, then breaks off another.

Training bakers for the new fifth shop, you have each of three people pinch a hundred dough balls and weigh every one; anything more than five grams off gets redone. They pinch until noon, their hands too sore to hold their bowls.

A supermarket chain in the east wants to stock the frozen dough, and its buyer comes with a test standard to negotiate. You turn the line's temperature logs and test reports page by page for him, and in the end what he asks is: will this dough get that rim in an oven at home?

The new pressing machine on the line leaves the rounds too thick in the middle, and they don't rise at the rim. You have the mold taken off, measure it bit by bit with calipers, and get two millimeters ground off.

Market regulators come for a spot check and take away three batches of dough. For the two days before the report, you look in on the retained samples in the lab every evening after work; only when the report comes back all clear do you go back to the old shop and bake a batch.
past: You grew up in Urumqi's old town, with this very naan shop downstairs. Every morning your mother gave you one yuan to go down and buy a hot naan for breakfast, and the old master always picked you the puffiest one.

You did badly in the high school entrance exam, and your father said go to a vocational school and learn a trade. You applied for Chinese pastry and learned flower rolls, steamed buns and leavened flatbreads, not one of them naan.
Kneading practice at school, you kneaded harder than anyone. At weekends you went downstairs to stand at the naan shop door and watch the old master bake, a whole morning at a time.
Your graduation placement was in a hotel pastry kitchen, making flaky pastries and cakes every day. You weren't bad at it, but the dough in your hands never felt like dough.

The day the placement ended, you went down to the naan shop and asked the old master if he'd take an apprentice. He looked at your arms and said: tend the fire and haul the flour first, and we'll talk about baking in a year.

The first time you baked a whole oven on your own, three fell off and two burned. The old master took the two burned ones and ate them himself; he wouldn't let you throw them away. That year you passed the Level 4 Chinese pastry certificate.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Urumqi's urban employee pension scheme. Naan shops mostly pay in on the minimum base, and there were gaps in your apprentice years, so in retirement you get about 40% of your last monthly salary; teaching at the training center brings in a separate income.
scenes: For the first month of retirement you still wake at four, lying there listening for someone pushing up a shutter downstairs. When you hear it, you turn over and fall asleep.

Your apprentice asks you back to the shop one morning a week. You don't bake; you stand at the side watching the young ones stamp patterns, and when someone's pattern goes crooked, you take the naan stamp from him and stamp a ring to show him.
Before your grandson goes to school, you go downstairs and buy him a hot naan, picking the puffiest one, the way the old master used to pick for you.

For the first few months away from the oven you couldn't sit still at home. Every morning you still walked to the shop door and stood a while, watching your apprentice open up and light the oven, and then went home.

A neighbor's family held a wedding and asked you to see to the big naan. You only stood by the oven and said a few words, and your apprentice did as you said; all thirty naan had the right patterns that day.

An old neighbor says the street in the old town has been redeveloped and all the shops have new signs. The naan shop is still there, its wooden rack by the door replaced with a glass cabinet. You went to see it once and bought a naan. It was still hot.
For the first month after leaving the old shop you woke at half past four on the dot, your hands under the quilt still making the motion of pressing out a round.
An apprentice you trained has opened his own naan shop in Changji and sent you a photo: his name on the sign over the door, and by the oven, an apprentice of his own.

The supermarket freezer holds a row of frozen naan dough, a tandoor oven printed on the pack. You took one home and baked it in the oven; your grandson said it was good, and you said it was still missing a ring of rim.

Lots of naan shops use temperature-controlled electric ovens now, and the big factories' lines turn out thousands an hour. But the people queuing at the door still need to watch a baker hook the naan out of the oven before it feels like naan to them.

Your right shoulder aches every winter, worn that way by decades of reaching into the oven. At New Year you still mix a tub of dough yourself and bake a few small naan in the electric oven at home for the children to take away.
You take your grandson round the bazaar, and passing a naan shop you stop at the door for a while, watching the young baker at work. After a long time you say his wrist is too stiff.

closing.retire: One morning many years later, you are mixing dough in the kitchen for your granddaughter, and before you know it you've pinched it into balls, all the same size. She asks why you don't use a scale. Your hand is the scale, you say.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you sit on a little stool outside the old shop in the sun, listening to the oven, and at one sound you know the fire is too high. You call out, and your apprentice's apprentice answers from inside.
closing.end: Many years later, sorting through old things, you find the naan stamp, its wooden handle still worn to a shine. You take a piece of dough, press it into a round on the table, stamp a ring of pattern, and leave it there, looking at it for a long time.
